`body.html` holds two to four pages, in this order. The template builds the top
navigation from each page's `data-title`, adds Back and Next links at the bottom
of every page, and shows one page at a time (the address bar's `#id` picks it).

| id | `data-title` | When | Reader | Length |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `short` | The short version | always | everyone, managers | one screen, about 1 minute |
| `how` | How it works | always | most readers | about 5 minutes, up to 5 sections |
| `show` | Show me | when something can be demonstrated | people who will do it | one or two walkthroughs |
| `deep` | Deep dive | when there is more worth knowing | the curious | as long as needed |

## The hierarchy rules

These decide what the eye sees first. The template's styles assume them.

1. **The answer comes first.** Page 1 states the conclusion. Each section on page 2
   opens with its point, then explains. Nothing builds up to a reveal.
2. **One orange thing per screen.** Orange (`hi`, `win`, `accent`) marks the single
   most important item in view: the key bar, the winning column, the current step.
   If two things are orange, neither stands out.
3. **Size and weight follow importance.** Headline, then section question, then
   body. Don't make secondary text big to fill space.
4. **Space separates; boxes are a last resort.** Thin lines and white space group
   things. Use a card only to hold an interactive part or a quick check.
5. **Every picture says what to notice.** A `.fig-note` beginning "What to notice:"
   under every figure.
6. **Pages stay short.** If "How it works" needs more than five sections, the extra
   ones belong in the deep dive.

## Page 1: the short version

```html
<section class="page" id="short" data-title="The short version">
  <div class="hero">
    <div class="wrap hero-grid">                      <!-- add "solo" to hero-grid if there is no hero figure -->
      <div>
        <p class="eyebrow">The short version · 1 minute</p>
        <h1><span class="ln"><span>The answer, as one statement.</span></span><span class="ln"><span class="soft">An optional second line in grey.</span></span></h1>
        <p class="dek">One sentence that adds the how.</p>
        <div class="big-number"><span class="num"><span class="count" style="--to:79"></span>%</span><small>what the number means, in one line</small></div>  <!-- optional -->
      </div>
      <figure class="fig hero-visual">                <!-- the one diagram that captures the whole idea -->
        <p class="fig-title"><span>Short title</span></p>
        …a diagram from diagrams.md…
        <p class="fig-note"><b>What to notice:</b> …</p>
      </figure>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="wrap">
    <ol class="takeaways">                           <!-- exactly three -->
      <li><span class="n">01</span><h3><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-target"/></svg>Takeaway in a few words</h3><p>One or two sentences.</p></li>
      <li>…</li>
      <li>…</li>
    </ol>
    <div class="so-what">
      <p class="eyebrow">What this means for you</p>
      <p>The decision, action or consequence, for this reader.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>
```

- Each `.ln` is one sentence of the headline; it rises into view when the page
  opens. Use at most two, and keep the whole headline to about 12 words: each
  sentence wraps onto two or three lines at desktop width.
- `.count` counts up to `--to`. Write units and symbols outside it, as in `~<span class="count" style="--to:60"></span> min`.
- Diagrams inside `.hero` switch to the night colours automatically.
- The hero figure should be simple: three to five elements, readable in seconds.

## Page 2: how it works

```html
<section class="page" id="how" data-title="How it works">
  <div class="words">                                <!-- "Words you'll meet": every term and abbreviation -->
    <div class="wrap">
      <p class="eyebrow">Words you'll meet</p>
      <dl class="words-grid">
        <div><dt>Access token</dt><dd>A short-lived digital key…</dd></div>
        <div><dt>Open Authorization (OAuth)</dt><dd>The open standard behind…</dd></div>
      </dl>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="wrap">
    <section class="section">                        <!-- up to five of these -->
      <div class="text">
        <p class="kicker">2.1</p>
        <h2>A question the reader would ask?</h2>
        <p>The point first. Then one or two short paragraphs.</p>
        <div class="analogy">An everyday comparison, if it helps.</div>     <!-- optional -->
      </div>
      <figure class="fig">
        <p class="fig-title"><span>What this diagram shows</span></p>
        …one diagram…
        <p class="fig-note"><b>What to notice:</b> the one thing to look at.</p>
      </figure>
      <details class="qc">                           <!-- quick check, spans both columns -->
        <summary><span class="qc-label">Quick check</span><span class="qc-q">A question about this section?</span><span class="qc-cta">Show answer</span></summary>
        <p class="ans">The answer, with the reason.</p>
      </details>
    </section>
  </div>
</section>
```

- "Words you'll meet" holds up to about eight terms. Needing more means the page
  leans on too much jargon: explain some in passing, or leave them out.
- `class="section wide"` puts the text above a full-width figure. Use it for wide
  diagrams, scroll stories, exploded views and maps.
- An inline definition, for a term not in the strip:
  `<span class="term" tabindex="0" data-def="Plain definition">term</span>`.
- Quick checks test the section's point, not trivia. In full mode, swap some of
  them for `.x-order` or `.x-predict` (see interactive.md); `.qc` stays fine too.
- Notes: `<div class="callout"><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-info"/></svg><div>…</div></div>`;
  add `warn` for a caution (with `#i-triangle-alert`).

## Page 3: show me

```html
<section class="page" id="show" data-title="Show me">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="page-intro">
      <p class="eyebrow">Show me</p>
      <h2>Watch it happen.</h2>
      <p>What the walkthrough shows, and that the reader can step through it.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="walk">…see showme.md…</div>
  </div>
</section>
```

## Page 4: deep dive

```html
<section class="page" id="deep" data-title="Deep dive">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="page-intro"><p class="eyebrow">Deep dive</p><h2>The details, for the curious.</h2><p>…</p></div>
    <section class="section wide">
      <div class="text"><h2>A question?</h2><p>…</p></div>
      …table, pros-cons, edge-cases, code, a diagram, or a full-mode exploded view or map…
    </section>
    <section class="section wide"><div class="text"><h2>Sources</h2></div><ol class="sources"><li><a href="…">…</a></li></ol></section>
  </div>
</section>
```

Building blocks for the deep dive (all in the template). Tables turn into
labelled rows on a phone automatically (the build copies each column heading onto
its cells), so keep them to about five columns and short cells:

```html
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead><tr><th>…</th><th class="num">…</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>…</td><td class="num">…</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<div class="pros-cons"><div><h3><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-thumbs-up"/></svg>Good for</h3><ul><li>…</li></ul></div><div><h3><svg class="ic"><use href="#i-thumbs-down"/></svg>Watch out for</h3><ul><li>…</li></ul></div></div>
<div class="edge-cases"><div><b>When X happens</b><p>What follows, in a sentence or two.</p></div></div>
<pre class="code"><span class="c"># a comment</span>
<span class="k">command</span> --flag value</pre>
```

## Motion

The template animates every figure once, when it scrolls into view, in reading
order. It adds a Replay link to each figure title and shows finished diagrams
when the reader asks for reduced motion. You don't write animation code.
Components animate by default, and the order follows the markup order, so put
items in the order you would explain them out loud.

### Pace

An explanatory animation is not interface motion: it has to be **followed**, not
just noticed. Fast animation shows the big picture and hides the details; slow
animation shows the details. Learners who are given the choice pick slow, and
older viewers struggle most with fast animation. So the template paces by reading:

| Token | Default | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `--beat` | 650 ms | the gap between **labelled** items (flow steps, cycle nodes, timeline items, cards, stack layers): long enough to read a short label before the next one appears |
| `--stagger` | 200 ms | the gap between **unlabelled marks** (bars, columns, segments), whose labels are already in place |
| `--tempo` | 1 | multiplies every duration and delay: `slow` is 1.5, `fast` 0.65 |

- **Choose the default pace** with `build_page.py --tempo slow|normal|fast`. Use `slow`
  for complex step-by-step builds, newcomers or older audiences, and `fast` for
  experts and simple pictures. The reader can always change it with the **Pace**
  button in the top bar, and their choice is remembered.
- **Walkthroughs** follow the pace too: each step's time, the cursor's glide and the
  typing speed are all multiplied by `--tempo`.
- **Long labels need longer.** Allow about a quarter of a second per word: put long
  labels in the prose, or give that item a longer delay.
- **Watch the shorthand.** `animation:` resets `animation-delay` to zero, so a
  shorthand declared after your delay makes every item appear at once. Add
  `class="paced"` to custom elements (with `style="--i:N"`) to get beat-paced
  delays that a shorthand can't override.
- **Custom CSS must follow the pace.** Write timings as
  `animation: rise calc(.8s * var(--tempo)) var(--ease) both;
  animation-delay: calc((var(--i) * var(--beat) + 200ms) * var(--tempo));`.
  The build warns about animation timings that ignore `--tempo`.

| What | At normal pace |
|---|---|
| One reveal (a bar growing, a box rising) | 0.7 to 1.2 seconds |
| Next labelled item | one beat (0.65 s) after the previous one; more for long labels |
| Next unlabelled mark | 0.2 seconds |
| A whole diagram | as long as reading it in order takes: 2 to 6 seconds is normal. Longer than about 8 seconds, it belongs in a walkthrough with step controls |

Never loop an animation while someone reads, never animate decoration, and never
hide content that only appears through animation.
